bull_thesis: Red Rock Resorts owns the best operating business in regional American gaming, and it owns the ground nobody else can build on. Its Las Vegas properties earned a 46.2% margin on revenue in 2025 - the share of each sales dollar left after running costs - against 22% to 35% across its peer group, and that gap widened rather than narrowed over five years. The reason is structural, not managerial luck: Nevada's gaming-district rules make new neighbourhood casino sites effectively unobtainable, and the 2025 annual report discloses roughly 454 acres of developable, gaming-entitled land across six Las Vegas parcels that Red Rock already controls. Most of it is described as shovel-ready. Nothing in the profit line captures that asset. The demand side is verifiable rather than asserted: the Las Vegas valley grows 1% to 1.5% a year while the one-mile ring around Downtown Summerlin grows over 6% and Summerlin West 3.6%, with roughly 34,000 new Summerlin households and 12,500 Henderson households still to arrive. On the 2026-04-29 call the customer looked healthy on every independent measure - the loyalty database grew in every age cohort, dining covers and average check both rose, and the out-of-town segment has now grown for ten consecutive quarters. The near-term earnings weakness is self-inflicted and reversible. Three properties are simultaneously under construction; management quantified 2025 disruption at roughly $20 million against $25 million guided, and the Green Valley Ranch towers have been offline for a full room-and-suite repositioning. When Green Valley Ranch reopens at a five-star room standard, Sunset Station's podium refresh finishes through 2026 and Durango North opens in summer 2027, the disruption reverses into growth on the same cost base. Capital allocation has been disciplined in the way that actually matters: 15.2 million shares retired at an average $45.53, well below today's price, with $573 million of authorisation running to December 2027, alongside a rising dividend and a $1 special dividend. Two contracted items sit outside the operating business entirely - a seven-year management agreement on the roughly $725 million North Fork Mono resort in Madera County, California, which management has guided to $40 million to $50 million of annual fees at stabilisation, and a note receivable of about $80 million accruing at the short-term reference rate plus 12 percentage points, which turns cash-paying the day the resort opens. Management has earned the benefit of the doubt on delivery: the December 2025 Durango expansion opened on budget and on schedule exactly as promised across three consecutive calls, construction disruption came in below guidance two years running, and the company has beaten consensus in seven of seven quarters. For this case to work, three conditions must hold: construction disruption must end on the stated timetable, the Durango cannibalisation backfill at the Red Rock property must complete by the late-2026 deadline management set itself, and North Fork must open in the autumn of 2026 and ramp toward the guided fee.
bear_thesis: The bear case here is not about business quality. It is about what you are being asked to pay, and about a balance sheet that removes the margin for error. Put those two corrections together and the market is paying about $6.8 billion of equity plus $3.44 billion of net debt, or roughly $10.2 billion of enterprise value, against $846 million of trailing operating cash profit. The March 2026 quarter broke a nine-quarter record streak: Las Vegas operating profit fell 1.5% year on year, consolidated fell 1.2%, and the margin gave back 129 basis points. Management never acknowledged that the streak ended; the language simply changed from records to resilience. # Red Rock Resorts (RRR) — Forensic Dossier

*Prepared 2026-07-27. Sources: five consecutive quarterly earnings calls (2025-05-01 through 2026-04-29), the screener's financial block, and live market data pulled today. Price used throughout: $65.06 per Class A share on the Nasdaq, in US dollars.*

---

## 0. A NECESSARY CORRECTION BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE

Three figures in the record handed to this committee are wrong, and all three are wrong in the same direction — they make the company look cheaper and safer than it is. They have to be fixed before a single valuation sentence is written.

**First, and most seriously: Red Rock does not have net cash. It carries about $3.44 billion of net debt.** The record states "net cash 64 million (cash 134 million exceeds total debt 70 million) — a genuine sum-of-the-parts add-back." That is a data-parsing failure. Management stated plainly on the 2026-04-29 call that at 31 March 2026 "the total principal amount of debt outstanding was $3.6 billion, resulting in net debt of $3.4 billion," and that net debt to earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA — a rough proxy for operating cash profit) stood at 4.07 times. The data feed correctly reported $3.41 billion of debt for the September 2025 quarter, then from December 2025 onward silently re-filed the long-term debt into an "other non-current liabilities" bucket of $3.59 billion, leaving a phantom $70 million debt total behind. The error is roughly $3.5 billion — about $33 per share on the company's full economic share count. Anyone who added that "net cash" to a valuation would have been wrong by half the market value of the company.

**Second, trailing free cash flow is not $598 million.** That figure is inflated by a sign error: fourth-quarter 2025 capital spending is recorded in the feed as a positive $265.9 million instead of the negative $78.9 million management actually reported, adding roughly $345 million of fictitious cash. Adding up the four real quarters, cash from operations less all capital spending was about $253 million over the trailing year. On management's own preferred measure — operating free cash flow, which is struck before growth projects — the trailing figure is about $491 million, or $4.70 per share.

**Third, there is no insider buying.** The record calls "13 buys (1,200,000 shares)" the "real conviction signal." Every acquisition in the company's Form 4 filings from November 2025 through June 2026 is either an equity award or an option exercise; every disposition is shares withheld to cover tax. There is not one open-market purchase in the file. On 11 June 2026, Frank and Lorenzo Fertitta each received 301,205 options struck at $62.32 plus 148,427 restricted shares. That is compensation, not conviction.

One more structural point that colours every per-share number below. Red Rock is what is known as an "up-C" company: the listed Class A shares (about 58.7 million) are only part of the economics. The Fertitta family holds units in the underlying operating company, Station Holdco, that convert one-for-one into Class A stock. Management's own per-share cash-flow arithmetic on every call uses the combined figure — roughly 104 million units as of the March 2026 quarter. The whole business, correctly measured, is 104 million units at $65.06, or about $6.8 billion of equity, plus $3.44 billion of net debt: an enterprise value near $10.2 billion. That is the number that matters, and it is nearly three times the market capitalisation the data feed reports.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across these five calls the story does not change. It compounds, and then — in the most recent quarter — it takes its first small step backwards.

The opening frame in **Q1 2025** is a company in the middle of a successful bet. Durango Casino & Resort, opened in December 2023, is "on pace to become one of our highest-margin properties," returning "nearly 16%" net of the business it stole from Red Rock's own flagship. The cannibalisation is acknowledged openly, and the promise is specific: "full revenue recovery over the next couple of years." Alongside it sits a construction slate — $120 million at Durango, $53 million at Sunset Station, $200 million at Green Valley Ranch — and a $750 million tribal project at North Fork in California, then guided to a "mid-2026 resort opening."

By **Q2 2025** the tone lifts to something close to triumph: "the best quarter in our company's history," the highest quarterly revenue and operating profit "in our 49-year history." Leverage falls below four times. The company pays a special dividend of $1 per share and buys back stock at an average $45.94.

**Q3 2025** introduces the story's one genuinely new chapter: a second, much larger Durango phase — 275,000 square feet, 400 more slot machines, a 36-lane bowling alley, cinemas, a country-western venue — at $385 million, breaking ground in January. North Fork's opening quietly moves from "mid-2026" to "Q4 '26." This slip is never called out as a slip; it simply appears in an answer about when the fees start.

**Q4 2025** is the peak of the narrative. Nine consecutive record quarters. More than $900 million of Las Vegas operating profit "for the first time in our 50-year history." A seventh consecutive quarter of falling leverage. Almost $297 million returned to shareholders in the year.

**Q1 2026** is where the arc bends. The language shifts, subtly but unmistakably, from records to resilience: the quarter delivered "the highest first quarter net revenue and the second highest first quarter adjusted EBITDA in our history" — note the demotion from first to second — "despite several headwinds later in the quarter including higher gas prices, air travel-related disruption and temporary construction impacts." Las Vegas operating profit fell 1.5% against the prior year. Leverage rose back to 4.07 times. The consecutive-record streak, celebrated in every prior script, simply vanishes from the prepared remarks. Nobody mentions that it ended.

What was quietly dropped: the specific Durango return figure (last given as "over 15%" in Q2 2025, absent thereafter), and the deleveraging streak. What was quietly added: a growing list of things to spend money on, and a leverage answer that now includes the phrase "we would spike leverage up."

## 2. CLAIMS versus FINANCIALS

Broken in March 2026: Las Vegas operating profit $232.4 million, down 1.5%; consolidated down 1.2%; margin down 129 basis points | **Was true, no longer true — and the change was not flagged** |

The honest all-units diluted figure for the March 2026 quarter is $0.42 against $0.75 a year earlier — down 44%.

---

## 3. TONE AND CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: High — with one qualification that materially changes how the beat record should be read.**

Red Rock does not guide earnings per share. It guides capital spending and construction disruption. Judge it on those.

*Disruption.* Guided at roughly $25 million for 2025; delivered below it, with the fourth quarter coming in at $5.1 million against $9.5 million flagged. Under-promised and over-delivered.

*Capital spending.* Guided at $350–400 million in May 2025, cut to $325–375 million in July, cut to $325–350 million in October, and finished the year at $319 million. Three consecutive downward revisions, each explained by "the timing of capital expenditures." That explanation is honest but it is also the tell: the spending did not go away, it moved into 2026, where the guide is now $375–425 million. The 2025 cash-flow conversion looked better than the underlying run-rate because roughly $60 million of spending was deferred into the following year.

*Project delivery.* The December 2025 Durango expansion opened on budget and on time, as promised across three consecutive calls. That is a real, checkable delivery. Against it, North Fork slid from "mid-2026" to "Q4 '26" without acknowledgement.

**The qualification on the beat record.** Seven beats out of seven, at margins of 35% to 137% above consensus, is not primarily evidence of management excellence. A company that beats by 137% is a company whose analysts are modelling something structurally different from what it reports — in this case, largely the up-C accounting and the swing items below operating profit. The beat rate should be read as a statement about the consensus estimate, not about management's execution. Judge execution on the disruption and capital numbers, where the record is genuinely good.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The vocabulary of the leverage answer changed.** In Q2 2025 the chief financial officer said "we've kind of knocked down leverage over the last several quarters just naturally through generating higher EBITDA." By Q1 2026 the same question produces "while we'd love to keep maintaining leverage on and around 4 for the right opportunities that we would spike leverage up." The frame moved from deleveraging-as-a-by-product to leverage-as-a-tool. Frank Fertitta's follow-on — listing North Fork, the $80 million note, Sunset and Green Valley as reasons profit will grow into the debt — is the classic argument for borrowing against a forecast.

**"Record" was replaced by "resilience."** Compare the Q2 2025 opener ("exceptional by every measure") with Q1 2026 ("underscoring the strength and resilience of our business model"). Resilience is the word a company reaches for when the number is not the story.

**Management pre-empted a demand question nobody had fully asked.** In Q1 2026 David Katz raised low-end consumer softness gently, and got an unusually emphatic three-executive rebuttal ending with Frank Fertitta's "it's not that our low end has been under pressure for a while... it's just been a pivot." The energy of the answer exceeded the pressure of the question. Read alongside "we're not in the promotion business anymore," the honest translation is that Red Rock has chosen to concede the value customer rather than defend them — a defensible strategy that also means the earnings base is more exposed to the affluent Las Vegas household than the headline "locals" framing suggests.

**Competitive framing is confident to the point of incuriosity.** Asked twice whether Strip operators are marketing into the locals market, the answer both times is a flat no, with Lorenzo Fertitta noting operators "have always taken a shot at locals... nothing has necessarily changed." That is probably right today. It is also the answer a market leader gives shortly before it stops being right.

**The taverns are a real strategic hedge, discussed too lightly.** Eight under contract, three open as of Q4 2025. Scott Kreeger is explicit that they exist to reach "a younger customer base." That is management telling you, without saying it, that the core resort database skews old — which is the one genuine long-run demand question this business faces.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT

**Trajectory: STABLE.**

Not strengthening: operating profit turned negative year over year in March 2026 for the first time in five years, leverage reversed direction, and revenue growth has flattened to under 1%. Not deteriorating: the decline is disclosed, self-inflicted by construction the company chose, and every independent measure of customer health — database growth, dining covers, average check, out-of-town visitation — is still positive.

**The single thing the director must weigh before sizing.** Red Rock is a high-quality operating business sitting on a balance sheet that removes the margin for error. At 4.07 times net debt to operating cash profit, with roughly $10.2 billion of enterprise value against $846 million of trailing profit, a one-and-a-half-turn multiple de-rating combined with a 7% profit decline roughly halves the equity. The company is committing $375–425 million of capital in 2026 and $385 million to Durango North through summer 2027, financed partly with debt, into a revenue line growing under 1% — while the Federal Reserve's priced base case is a rate hike, not a cut, and management's own named headwind (fuel prices) is actively worsening. The quality of the franchise is not in question. The question is entirely whether the price leaves anything for the buyer.

**Economic moat: WIDE, and stable rather than widening.** The moat type is a regulatory licence combined with irreplaceable location. Nevada's gaming-district rules mean new locals casinos can effectively only be built on grandfathered, gaming-entitled parcels, and Red Rock owns 454 acres of them across six sites. The evidence that this is real and not merely asserted is in the margin: 46.2% at the property level for 2025 and rising, against a peer group at 22% to 35%. That is not a small edge; it is a structural one, and it has widened over five years, not narrowed. The most recent quarter's 113 basis-point margin decline is construction disruption at three named properties, not competitive erosion, and does not make this an eroding moat. It is marked stable rather than widening because revenue growth has stalled below 1% and returns on invested capital, at roughly 14%, are flat — good, above the cost of capital, but not compounding upward. One honest caveat: a moat that a company breaches itself is a location moat, not a franchise moat. Durango cannibalised Red Rock's own flagship badly enough to need a three-year recovery plan. The protection is against outsiders, not against the company's own next building.

**Secular threat: manageable.** There is no structural force visibly melting this earnings base. The Las Vegas valley is growing; the specific submarkets Red Rock sits in are growing faster. Online casino gaming is the theoretical threat, and Nevada is the state least likely to authorise it, since it would cannibalise the tax base the state depends on. The genuine long-run question — flagged by management's own tavern strategy — is generational: whether the next cohort of Las Vegas households treats a neighbourhood casino as their default entertainment the way the current one does. That is a real question, but it is a slow one, and nothing in these five quarters suggests it is biting yet.

**So: fear-print or value trap? Neither.** This is the third case, and it is the one the screener's corrupted inputs obscured. Red Rock is not cheap and it is not melting. It is a genuinely excellent, genuinely protected business trading at roughly twelve times enterprise value to trailing operating profit — above the highest-quality small-cap peer in its group, which carries net cash rather than $3.4 billion of net debt. The optical cheapness in the record was an artefact of three data errors. Corrected, there is no discount here to buy. There is a fine business at a full price, with the leverage to punish a disappointment.

# Red Rock Resorts (RRR) — Forensic Dossier

*Prepared 2026-07-27. Sources: five consecutive quarterly earnings calls (2025-05-01 through 2026-04-29), the screener's financial block, and live market data pulled today. Price used throughout: $65.06 per Class A share on the Nasdaq, in US dollars.*

---

## 0. A NECESSARY CORRECTION BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE

Three figures in the record handed to this committee are wrong, and all three are wrong in the same direction — they make the company look cheaper and safer than it is. They have to be fixed before a single valuation sentence is written.

**First, and most seriously: Red Rock does not have net cash. It carries about $3.44 billion of net debt.** The record states "net cash 64 million (cash 134 million exceeds total debt 70 million) — a genuine sum-of-the-parts add-back." That is a data-parsing failure. Management stated plainly on the 2026-04-29 call that at 31 March 2026 "the total principal amount of debt outstanding was $3.6 billion, resulting in net debt of $3.4 billion," and that net debt to earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA — a rough proxy for operating cash profit) stood at 4.07 times. The data feed correctly reported $3.41 billion of debt for the September 2025 quarter, then from December 2025 onward silently re-filed the long-term debt into an "other non-current liabilities" bucket of $3.59 billion, leaving a phantom $70 million debt total behind. The error is roughly $3.5 billion — about $33 per share on the company's full economic share count. Anyone who added that "net cash" to a valuation would have been wrong by half the market value of the company.

**Second, trailing free cash flow is not $598 million.** That figure is inflated by a sign error: fourth-quarter 2025 capital spending is recorded in the feed as a positive $265.9 million instead of the negative $78.9 million management actually reported, adding roughly $345 million of fictitious cash. Adding up the four real quarters, cash from operations less all capital spending was about $253 million over the trailing year. On management's own preferred measure — operating free cash flow, which is struck before growth projects — the trailing figure is about $491 million, or $4.70 per share.

**Third, there is no insider buying.** The record calls "13 buys (1,200,000 shares)" the "real conviction signal." Every acquisition in the company's Form 4 filings from November 2025 through June 2026 is either an equity award or an option exercise; every disposition is shares withheld to cover tax. There is not one open-market purchase in the file. On 11 June 2026, Frank and Lorenzo Fertitta each received 301,205 options struck at $62.32 plus 148,427 restricted shares. That is compensation, not conviction.

One more structural point that colours every per-share number below. Red Rock is what is known as an "up-C" company: the listed Class A shares (about 58.7 million) are only part of the economics. The Fertitta family holds units in the underlying operating company, Station Holdco, that convert one-for-one into Class A stock. Management's own per-share cash-flow arithmetic on every call uses the combined figure — roughly 104 million units as of the March 2026 quarter. The whole business, correctly measured, is 104 million units at $65.06, or about $6.8 billion of equity, plus $3.44 billion of net debt: an enterprise value near $10.2 billion. That is the number that matters, and it is nearly three times the market capitalisation the data feed reports.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across these five calls the story does not change. It compounds, and then — in the most recent quarter — it takes its first small step backwards.

The opening frame in **Q1 2025** is a company in the middle of a successful bet. Durango Casino & Resort, opened in December 2023, is "on pace to become one of our highest-margin properties," returning "nearly 16%" net of the business it stole from Red Rock's own flagship. The cannibalisation is acknowledged openly, and the promise is specific: "full revenue recovery over the next couple of years." Alongside it sits a construction slate — $120 million at Durango, $53 million at Sunset Station, $200 million at Green Valley Ranch — and a $750 million tribal project at North Fork in California, then guided to a "mid-2026 resort opening."

By **Q2 2025** the tone lifts to something close to triumph: "the best quarter in our company's history," the highest quarterly revenue and operating profit "in our 49-year history." Leverage falls below four times. The company pays a special dividend of $1 per share and buys back stock at an average $45.94.

**Q3 2025** introduces the story's one genuinely new chapter: a second, much larger Durango phase — 275,000 square feet, 400 more slot machines, a 36-lane bowling alley, cinemas, a country-western venue — at $385 million, breaking ground in January. North Fork's opening quietly moves from "mid-2026" to "Q4 '26." This slip is never called out as a slip; it simply appears in an answer about when the fees start.

**Q4 2025** is the peak of the narrative. Nine consecutive record quarters. More than $900 million of Las Vegas operating profit "for the first time in our 50-year history." A seventh consecutive quarter of falling leverage. Almost $297 million returned to shareholders in the year.

The language shifts, subtly but unmistakably, from records to resilience: the quarter delivered "the highest first quarter net revenue and the second highest first quarter adjusted EBITDA in our history" — note the demotion from first to second — "despite several headwinds later in the quarter including higher gas prices, air travel-related disruption and temporary construction impacts." The consecutive-record streak, celebrated in every prior script, simply vanishes from the prepared remarks. Nobody mentions that it ended.

What was quietly dropped: the specific Durango return figure (last given as "over 15%" in Q2 2025, absent thereafter), and the deleveraging streak. What was quietly added: a growing list of things to spend money on, and a leverage answer that now includes the phrase "we would spike leverage up."

**Rating: Stable, with a clear step down in the most recent quarter.**

- *Q3 2025 — confident and expansionary.* The $385 million Durango phase is announced with an explicit return promise from Lorenzo Fertitta: "low teens, growing to mid-teens and eventually growing to kind of our 20% threshold."
- *Q4 2025 — confident, with the first defensive note.* Asked about cost inflation, the answer turns operational: labour "mid-single digits," insurance "tail wagging the dog." Still offensive, but the questions are now about costs.
- *Q1 2026 — resilient, not triumphant.* "Underscoring the strength and resilience of our business model." Three external headwinds are named in the opening paragraph. The word "despite" carries the sentence. On leverage, the chief financial officer's answer now contemplates going up rather than down: "for the right opportunities that we would spike leverage up." That is a real shift in posture, from a team paying down debt to a team reserving the right to add it.

On specificity, management is unusually good and stays good: they quantify disruption by property and by quarter, they give per-share cash-flow figures, they name the return threshold on each project. They do not give earnings guidance, which matters for section 4.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: High — with one qualification that materially changes how the beat record should be read.**

Red Rock does not guide earnings per share. It guides capital spending and construction disruption. Judge it on those.

*Disruption.* Guided at roughly $25 million for 2025; delivered below it, with the fourth quarter coming in at $5.1 million against $9.5 million flagged. Under-promised and over-delivered.

*Capital spending.* Guided at $350–400 million in May 2025, cut to $325–375 million in July, cut to $325–350 million in October, and finished the year at $319 million. Three consecutive downward revisions, each explained by "the timing of capital expenditures." That explanation is honest but it is also the tell: the spending did not go away, it moved into 2026, where the guide is now $375–425 million. The 2025 cash-flow conversion looked better than the underlying run-rate because roughly $60 million of spending was deferred into the following year.

*Project delivery.* The December 2025 Durango expansion opened on budget and on time, as promised across three consecutive calls. That is a real, checkable delivery. Against it, North Fork slid from "mid-2026" to "Q4 '26" without acknowledgement.

**The qualification on the beat record.** Seven beats out of seven, at margins of 35% to 137% above consensus, is not primarily evidence of management excellence. A company that beats by 137% is a company whose analysts are modelling something structurally different from what it reports — in this case, largely the up-C accounting and the swing items below operating profit. The beat rate should be read as a statement about the consensus estimate, not about management's execution. Judge execution on the disruption and capital numbers, where the record is genuinely good.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**What analysts keep circling, and what management does with it:**

*The Durango backfill.* Asked in some form on four of five calls. The answers are consistently qualitative — "we're on track," "we're kind of in the year 2 in the throes of year 2," "our core properties are growing low single digits" — and never quantitative. Management has not once said what Red Rock property revenue actually is against its pre-Durango base. The three-year deadline they set themselves in December 2023 falls due at the end of 2026. This is the single most deflected question in the file.

*Leverage capacity.* David Katz (Jefferies) asked the ideal leverage range in Q2 2025; Chad Beynon (Macquarie) asked the maximum in Q1 2026. Both answers avoid a number. The closest thing to a ceiling is a sentence fragment — "I think once you start topping — that's really where you start kind of — kind of you start getting a little concerned." A management team with a firm leverage policy states it. This one does not.

*Returns on the $385 million Durango phase.* Brandt Montour (Barclays) asked directly for a gaming versus non-gaming breakdown to model the return. Lorenzo Fertitta declined the breakdown and offered an aspiration instead. For a project this size — roughly 45% of a year's operating cash profit — a refusal to decompose the return is a fair thing for a capital allocator to note.

*What analysts are not yet pressing on.* Nobody has asked why adjusted profit includes a non-cash development-fee accrual. Nobody has asked what happens to reported profit when that accrual stops at North Fork's opening. And nobody has asked management to reconcile "we would spike leverage up" with a starting point of 4.07 times.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS AND GREEN FLAGS

**Concerning:**

- *The streak ended and nobody said so (Q1 2026).* Las Vegas operating profit fell 1.5%; the nine-quarter record language, present in every prior script, was deleted rather than addressed.
- *Deleveraging reversed in one quarter (Q1 2026).* From 3.87 to 4.07 times, with $147.8 million of new net borrowing. - *A non-cash accrual inside the headline profit measure (all four quarters).* About $20.5 million over the trailing year, disclosed but not separated from the record claims.
- *The Durango return figure quietly walked down* from "nearly 16%" (Q1 2025) to "over 15%" (Q2 2025), then disappeared.
- *A widening spending commitment into a flattening revenue line.* Las Vegas revenue growth: +1.9%, +6.2%, +1.0%, +2.5%, +0.9% across the five quarters. The last figure is the smallest, and the capital budget is the largest.

Brent crude is roughly $89 as of the most recent market read, up about 24% from early July on the reinstated Hormuz blockade. The California drive-in customer that management described in Q1 2025 as enjoying a "cheap date" is getting a more expensive one.
- *No open-market insider purchase in the file,* while the controlling family received roughly 600,000 options and 297,000 restricted shares in a single June 2026 grant.

**Positive:**

- *Margins that no peer approaches.* 46.2% Las Vegas property margin for 2025, up year on year, against 22% to 35% across the regional casino peer group. - *Real, independent evidence the customer is healthy.* Database growth in every age cohort; food and beverage covers and average check both up in the most recent quarter — and management is right that discretionary dining is the honest bellwether; the out-of-town segment growing ten consecutive quarters.
- *A serious, disciplined buyback.* 15.2 million shares retired at an average $45.53 — well below today's price — with $573 million of authorisation running to December 2027. That is buying low, which is rarer than it should be.

**The vocabulary of the leverage answer changed.** In Q2 2025 the chief financial officer said "we've kind of knocked down leverage over the last several quarters just naturally through generating higher EBITDA." By Q1 2026 the same question produces "while we'd love to keep maintaining leverage on and around 4 for the right opportunities that we would spike leverage up." The frame moved from deleveraging-as-a-by-product to leverage-as-a-tool. Frank Fertitta's follow-on — listing North Fork, the $80 million note, Sunset and Green Valley as reasons profit will grow into the debt — is the classic argument for borrowing against a forecast.

**"Record" was replaced by "resilience."** Compare the Q2 2025 opener ("exceptional by every measure") with Q1 2026 ("underscoring the strength and resilience of our business model"). Resilience is the word a company reaches for when the number is not the story.

**Management pre-empted a demand question nobody had fully asked.** In Q1 2026 David Katz raised low-end consumer softness gently, and got an unusually emphatic three-executive rebuttal ending with Frank Fertitta's "it's not that our low end has been under pressure for a while... it's just been a pivot." ## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT

**Trajectory: STABLE.**

Not strengthening: operating profit turned negative year over year in March 2026 for the first time in five years, leverage reversed direction, and revenue growth has flattened to under 1%. Not deteriorating: the decline is disclosed, self-inflicted by construction the company chose, and every independent measure of customer health — database growth, dining covers, average check, out-of-town visitation — is still positive.

**The single thing the director must weigh before sizing.** Red Rock is a high-quality operating business sitting on a balance sheet that removes the margin for error. At 4.07 times net debt to operating cash profit, with roughly $10.2 billion of enterprise value against $846 million of trailing profit, a one-and-a-half-turn multiple de-rating combined with a 7% profit decline roughly halves the equity. The company is committing $375–425 million of capital in 2026 and $385 million to Durango North through summer 2027, financed partly with debt, into a revenue line growing under 1% — while the Federal Reserve's priced base case is a rate hike, not a cut, and management's own named headwind (fuel prices) is actively worsening. The quality of the franchise is not in question. The question is entirely whether the price leaves anything for the buyer.

**Economic moat: WIDE, and stable rather than widening.** The moat type is a regulatory licence combined with irreplaceable location. Nevada's gaming-district rules mean new locals casinos can effectively only be built on grandfathered, gaming-entitled parcels, and Red Rock owns 454 acres of them across six sites. The evidence that this is real and not merely asserted is in the margin: 46.2% at the property level for 2025 and rising, against a peer group at 22% to 35%. That is not a small edge; it is a structural one, and it has widened over five years, not narrowed. The most recent quarter's 113 basis-point margin decline is construction disruption at three named properties, not competitive erosion, and does not make this an eroding moat. It is marked stable rather than widening because revenue growth has stalled below 1% and returns on invested capital, at roughly 14%, are flat — good, above the cost of capital, but not compounding upward. One honest caveat: a moat that a company breaches itself is a location moat, not a franchise moat. Durango cannibalised Red Rock's own flagship badly enough to need a three-year recovery plan. The protection is against outsiders, not against the company's own next building.

**Secular threat: manageable.** There is no structural force visibly melting this earnings base. The Las Vegas valley is growing; the specific submarkets Red Rock sits in are growing faster. Online casino gaming is the theoretical threat, and Nevada is the state least likely to authorise it, since it would cannibalise the tax base the state depends on. The genuine long-run question — flagged by management's own tavern strategy — is generational: whether the next cohort of Las Vegas households treats a neighbourhood casino as their default entertainment the way the current one does. That is a real question, but it is a slow one, and nothing in these five quarters suggests it is biting yet.

**So: fear-print or value trap? Neither.** This is the third case, and it is the one the screener's corrupted inputs obscured. Red Rock is not cheap and it is not melting. It is a genuinely excellent, genuinely protected business trading at roughly twelve times enterprise value to trailing operating profit — above the highest-quality small-cap peer in its group, which carries net cash rather than $3.4 billion of net debt. The optical cheapness in the record was an artefact of three data errors. Corrected, there is no discount here to buy. There is a fine business at a full price, with the leverage to punish a disappointment.

interrogator_dossier:
# Red Rock Resorts (RRR) — Forensic Dossier

*Prepared 2026-07-27. Sources: five consecutive quarterly earnings calls (2025-05-01 through 2026-04-29), the screener's financial block, and live market data pulled today. Price used throughout: $65.06 per Class A share on the Nasdaq, in US dollars.*

---

## 0. A NECESSARY CORRECTION BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE

Three figures in the record handed to this committee are wrong, and all three are wrong in the same direction — they make the company look cheaper and safer than it is. They have to be fixed before a single valuation sentence is written.

**First, and most seriously: Red Rock does not have net cash. It carries about $3.44 billion of net debt.** The record states "net cash 64 million (cash 134 million exceeds total debt 70 million) — a genuine sum-of-the-parts add-back." That is a data-parsing failure. Management stated plainly on the 2026-04-29 call that at 31 March 2026 "the total principal amount of debt outstanding was $3.6 billion, resulting in net debt of $3.4 billion," and that net debt to earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA — a rough proxy for operating cash profit) stood at 4.07 times. The data feed correctly reported $3.41 billion of debt for the September 2025 quarter, then from December 2025 onward silently re-filed the long-term debt into an "other non-current liabilities" bucket of $3.59 billion, leaving a phantom $70 million debt total behind. The error is roughly $3.5 billion — about $33 per share on the company's full economic share count. Anyone who added that "net cash" to a valuation would have been wrong by half the market value of the company.

**Second, trailing free cash flow is not $598 million.** That figure is inflated by a sign error: fourth-quarter 2025 capital spending is recorded in the feed as a positive $265.9 million instead of the negative $78.9 million management actually reported, adding roughly $345 million of fictitious cash. Adding up the four real quarters, cash from operations less all capital spending was about $253 million over the trailing year. On management's own preferred measure — operating free cash flow, which is struck before growth projects — the trailing figure is about $491 million, or $4.70 per share.

**Third, there is no insider buying.** The record calls "13 buys (1,200,000 shares)" the "real conviction signal." Every acquisition in the company's Form 4 filings from November 2025 through June 2026 is either an equity award or an option exercise; every disposition is shares withheld to cover tax. There is not one open-market purchase in the file. On 11 June 2026, Frank and Lorenzo Fertitta each received 301,205 options struck at $62.32 plus 148,427 restricted shares. That is compensation, not conviction.

One more structural point that colours every per-share number below. Red Rock is what is known as an "up-C" company: the listed Class A shares (about 58.7 million) are only part of the economics. The Fertitta family holds units in the underlying operating company, Station Holdco, that convert one-for-one into Class A stock. Management's own per-share cash-flow arithmetic on every call uses the combined figure — roughly 104 million units as of the March 2026 quarter. The whole business, correctly measured, is 104 million units at $65.06, or about $6.8 billion of equity, plus $3.44 billion of net debt: an enterprise value near $10.2 billion. That is the number that matters, and it is nearly three times the market capitalisation the data feed reports.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across these five calls the story does not change. It compounds, and then — in the most recent quarter — it takes its first small step backwards.

The opening frame in **Q1 2025** is a company in the middle of a successful bet. Durango Casino & Resort, opened in December 2023, is "on pace to become one of our highest-margin properties," returning "nearly 16%" net of the business it stole from Red Rock's own flagship. The cannibalisation is acknowledged openly, and the promise is specific: "full revenue recovery over the next couple of years." Alongside it sits a construction slate — $120 million at Durango, $53 million at Sunset Station, $200 million at Green Valley Ranch — and a $750 million tribal project at North Fork in California, then guided to a "mid-2026 resort opening."

By **Q2 2025** the tone lifts to something close to triumph: "the best quarter in our company's history," the highest quarterly revenue and operating profit "in our 49-year history." Leverage falls below four times. The company pays a special dividend of $1 per share and buys back stock at an average $45.94.

**Q3 2025** introduces the story's one genuinely new chapter: a second, much larger Durango phase — 275,000 square feet, 400 more slot machines, a 36-lane bowling alley, cinemas, a country-western venue — at $385 million, breaking ground in January. North Fork's opening quietly moves from "mid-2026" to "Q4 '26." This slip is never called out as a slip; it simply appears in an answer about when the fees start.

**Q4 2025** is the peak of the narrative. Nine consecutive record quarters. More than $900 million of Las Vegas operating profit "for the first time in our 50-year history." A seventh consecutive quarter of falling leverage. Almost $297 million returned to shareholders in the year.

**Q1 2026** is where the arc bends. The language shifts, subtly but unmistakably, from records to resilience: the quarter delivered "the highest first quarter net revenue and the second highest first quarter adjusted EBITDA in our history" — note the demotion from first to second — "despite several headwinds later in the quarter including higher gas prices, air travel-related disruption and temporary construction impacts." Las Vegas operating profit fell 1.5% against the prior year. Leverage rose back to 4.07 times. The consecutive-record streak, celebrated in every prior script, simply vanishes from the prepared remarks. Nobody mentions that it ended.

What was quietly dropped: the specific Durango return figure (last given as "over 15%" in Q2 2025, absent thereafter), and the deleveraging streak. What was quietly added: a growing list of things to spend money on, and a leverage answer that now includes the phrase "we would spike leverage up."

---

## 2. CLAIMS versus FINANCIALS

| Management's claim | The evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Nine consecutive record quarters" of revenue and operating profit (Q4 2025) | True through December 2025. Broken in March 2026: Las Vegas operating profit $232.4 million, down 1.5%; consolidated down 1.2%; margin down 129 basis points | **Was true, no longer true — and the change was not flagged** |
| Best-in-class margins, "the 20th quarter of the 22 that we've hit above 45%" in Las Vegas (Q4 2025) | Full-year 2025 Las Vegas margin 46.2%, up 56 basis points. Peer property margins run roughly 22% to 35%. This is the single most impressive number in the file | **Verified, and genuinely exceptional** |
| Construction disruption of roughly $25 million for 2025 | Came in "better than we thought" — the fourth quarter alone was guided at $9.5 million and landed at $5.1 million | **Delivered, with room to spare** |
| "Seventh consecutive quarter of deleveraging" (Q4 2025) | 3.87 times at December 2025. Then 4.07 times at March 2026, financed by $147.8 million of fresh net borrowing in a single quarter | **True on the day, reversed one quarter later** |
| Free cash flow "converted 55% of our adjusted EBITDA," $466.3 million or $4.44 per share for 2025 | Arithmetically consistent, and the per-share divisor confirms the ~105 million combined unit count. But this measure is struck before growth capital. After all capital spending, trailing free cash flow is roughly $253 million | **Accurate as defined — but the definition does a lot of work** |
| Durango "return net of cannibalization of nearly 16%" (Q1 2025) | Restated as "over 15%" one quarter later, then never quantified again | **A quiet one-point walk-down, unacknowledged** |
| Earnings consistently ahead of expectations | Confirmed: seven of seven, and by wide margins — $0.73 against $0.54 expected in Q1 2026; $0.75 against $0.41; $0.68 against $0.36; $0.95 against $0.40 | **Verified — but see section 4 on what this actually proves** |
| The core business is healthy | Corroborated across independent lines: database grew in every age cohort (Q4 2025); food and beverage covers and average check both up (Q1 2026); the out-of-town customer segment up ten straight quarters | **Verified** |

**Where the story is richer than the numbers justify.** The "record adjusted EBITDA" framing leans, quietly, on a non-cash item. Management has been accruing a North Fork development fee into consolidated adjusted profit: $10 million in the June 2025 quarter, then $3.9 million, $3.7 million and $2.9 million — about $20.5 million over the trailing year, roughly 2.4% of the headline. Management said plainly this "obviously is non-cash." It is nonetheless inside the number that supports the record language and the leverage ratio. Strip it out and the trailing operating cash profit is about $825 million rather than $846 million.

**Where the numbers are richer than the story.** The screener's return-on-equity figure of 228% and its earnings-per-share growth of +23% are artefacts of the up-C structure, not real. Class A book equity is only $142.7 million because most of the economics sit outside it in the non-controlling interest. The honest all-units diluted figure for the March 2026 quarter is $0.42 against $0.75 a year earlier — down 44%.

---

## 3. TONE AND CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Stable, with a clear step down in the most recent quarter.**

- *Q1 2025 — confident, forward-leaning.* "The first quarter represented another strong quarter for the Company by all measures." Growth language dominates; every project gets a return target.
- *Q2 2025 — peak confidence.* "The second quarter was an exceptional one for the company by every measure." Superlatives are unhedged. The special dividend and buyback are the actions of a management team that believes its own numbers.
- *Q3 2025 — confident and expansionary.* The $385 million Durango phase is announced with an explicit return promise from Lorenzo Fertitta: "low teens, growing to mid-teens and eventually growing to kind of our 20% threshold."
- *Q4 2025 — confident, with the first defensive note.* Asked about cost inflation, the answer turns operational: labour "mid-single digits," insurance "tail wagging the dog." Still offensive, but the questions are now about costs.
- *Q1 2026 — resilient, not triumphant.* "Underscoring the strength and resilience of our business model." Three external headwinds are named in the opening paragraph. The word "despite" carries the sentence. On leverage, the chief financial officer's answer now contemplates going up rather than down: "for the right opportunities that we would spike leverage up." That is a real shift in posture, from a team paying down debt to a team reserving the right to add it.

On specificity, management is unusually good and stays good: they quantify disruption by property and by quarter, they give per-share cash-flow figures, they name the return threshold on each project. They do not give earnings guidance, which matters for section 4.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: High — with one qualification that materially changes how the beat record should be read.**

Red Rock does not guide earnings per share. It guides capital spending and construction disruption. Judge it on those.

*Disruption.* Guided at roughly $25 million for 2025; delivered below it, with the fourth quarter coming in at $5.1 million against $9.5 million flagged. Under-promised and over-delivered.

*Capital spending.* Guided at $350–400 million in May 2025, cut to $325–375 million in July, cut to $325–350 million in October, and finished the year at $319 million. Three consecutive downward revisions, each explained by "the timing of capital expenditures." That explanation is honest but it is also the tell: the spending did not go away, it moved into 2026, where the guide is now $375–425 million. The 2025 cash-flow conversion looked better than the underlying run-rate because roughly $60 million of spending was deferred into the following year.

*Project delivery.* The December 2025 Durango expansion opened on budget and on time, as promised across three consecutive calls. That is a real, checkable delivery. Against it, North Fork slid from "mid-2026" to "Q4 '26" without acknowledgement.

**The qualification on the beat record.** Seven beats out of seven, at margins of 35% to 137% above consensus, is not primarily evidence of management excellence. A company that beats by 137% is a company whose analysts are modelling something structurally different from what it reports — in this case, largely the up-C accounting and the swing items below operating profit. The beat rate should be read as a statement about the consensus estimate, not about management's execution. Judge execution on the disruption and capital numbers, where the record is genuinely good.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**What analysts keep circling, and what management does with it:**

*The Durango backfill.* Asked in some form on four of five calls. The answers are consistently qualitative — "we're on track," "we're kind of in the year 2 in the throes of year 2," "our core properties are growing low single digits" — and never quantitative. Management has not once said what Red Rock property revenue actually is against its pre-Durango base. The three-year deadline they set themselves in December 2023 falls due at the end of 2026. This is the single most deflected question in the file.

*Leverage capacity.* David Katz (Jefferies) asked the ideal leverage range in Q2 2025; Chad Beynon (Macquarie) asked the maximum in Q1 2026. Both answers avoid a number. The closest thing to a ceiling is a sentence fragment — "I think once you start topping — that's really where you start kind of — kind of you start getting a little concerned." A management team with a firm leverage policy states it. This one does not.

*Returns on the $385 million Durango phase.* Brandt Montour (Barclays) asked directly for a gaming versus non-gaming breakdown to model the return. *What analysts are not yet pressing on.* Nobody has asked why adjusted profit includes a non-cash development-fee accrual. Nobody has asked what happens to reported profit when that accrual stops at North Fork's opening. And nobody has asked management to reconcile "we would spike leverage up" with a starting point of 4.07 times.

## 6. RED FLAGS AND GREEN FLAGS

**Concerning:**

- *The streak ended and nobody said so (Q1 2026).* Las Vegas operating profit fell 1.5%; the nine-quarter record language, present in every prior script, was deleted rather than addressed.
- *Deleveraging reversed in one quarter (Q1 2026).* From 3.87 to 4.07 times, with $147.8 million of new net borrowing. In the same quarter the company returned $170.5 million to shareholders against $22.6 million of free cash flow after all capital spending. Shareholder returns were, arithmetically, debt-funded.
- *A non-cash accrual inside the headline profit measure (all four quarters).* About $20.5 million over the trailing year, disclosed but not separated from the record claims.
- *The Durango return figure quietly walked down* from "nearly 16%" (Q1 2025) to "over 15%" (Q2 2025), then disappeared.
- *A widening spending commitment into a flattening revenue line.* Las Vegas revenue growth: +1.9%, +6.2%, +1.0%, +2.5%, +0.9% across the five quarters. The last figure is the smallest, and the capital budget is the largest.
- *Management's own named headwind is live and worsening.* Q1 2026 cited "higher gas prices." Brent crude is roughly $89 as of the most recent market read, up about 24% from early July on the reinstated Hormuz blockade. The California drive-in customer that management described in Q1 2025 as enjoying a "cheap date" is getting a more expensive one.
- *No open-market insider purchase in the file,* while the controlling family received roughly 600,000 options and 297,000 restricted shares in a single June 2026 grant.

**Positive:**

- *Margins that no peer approaches.* 46.2% Las Vegas property margin for 2025, up year on year, against 22% to 35% across the regional casino peer group. Management attributes it to a deliberate post-pandemic pivot away from promotional spending toward high-limit slots and tables — and the numbers corroborate the story.
- *Delivery on the things they promised to deliver.* Durango's December 2025 expansion: on budget, on schedule, across three calls. Disruption below guidance two years running.
- *Real, independent evidence the customer is healthy.* Database growth in every age cohort; food and beverage covers and average check both up in the most recent quarter — and management is right that discretionary dining is the honest bellwether; the out-of-town segment growing ten consecutive quarters.
- *A serious, disciplined buyback.* 15.2 million shares retired at an average $45.53 — well below today's price — with $573 million of authorisation running to December 2027. That is buying low, which is rarer than it should be.
- *Genuine asset scarcity.* The 2025 annual report discloses roughly 454 acres of developable, gaming-entitled land across six Las Vegas parcels. In a market where new casino entitlements are effectively unobtainable, that is a real, unearning asset the profit line does not capture.
- *Demographics that are actually verifiable.* Summerlin West growing 3.6% and the one-mile ring around Downtown Summerlin over 6%, against a valley growing 1% to 1.5%. Roughly 34,000 new households in Summerlin and 12,500 in Henderson at full build-out.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The vocabulary of the leverage answer changed.** In Q2 2025 the chief financial officer said "we've kind of knocked down leverage over the last several quarters just naturally through generating higher EBITDA." By Q1 2026 the same question produces "while we'd love to keep maintaining leverage on and around 4 for the right opportunities that we would spike leverage up." The frame moved from deleveraging-as-a-by-product to leverage-as-a-tool. Frank Fertitta's follow-on — listing North Fork, the $80 million note, Sunset and Green Valley as reasons profit will grow into the debt — is the classic argument for borrowing against a forecast.

**"Record" was replaced by "resilience."** Compare the Q2 2025 opener ("exceptional by every measure") with Q1 2026 ("underscoring the strength and resilience of our business model"). Resilience is the word a company reaches for when the number is not the story.

**Management pre-empted a demand question nobody had fully asked.** In Q1 2026 David Katz raised low-end consumer softness gently, and got an unusually emphatic three-executive rebuttal ending with Frank Fertitta's "it's not that our low end has been under pressure for a while... it's just been a pivot." The energy of the answer exceeded the pressure of the question. Read alongside "we're not in the promotion business anymore," the honest translation is that Red Rock has chosen to concede the value customer rather than defend them — a defensible strategy that also means the earnings base is more exposed to the affluent Las Vegas household than the headline "locals" framing suggests.

**Competitive framing is confident to the point of incuriosity.** Asked twice whether Strip operators are marketing into the locals market, the answer both times is a flat no, with Lorenzo Fertitta noting operators "have always taken a shot at locals... nothing has necessarily changed." That is probably right today. It is also the answer a market leader gives shortly before it stops being right.

**The taverns are a real strategic hedge, discussed too lightly.** Eight under contract, three open as of Q4 2025. Scott Kreeger is explicit that they exist to reach "a younger customer base." That is management telling you, without saying it, that the core resort database skews old — which is the one genuine long-run demand question this business faces.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT

**Trajectory: STABLE.**

Not strengthening: operating profit turned negative year over year in March 2026 for the first time in five years, leverage reversed direction, and revenue growth has flattened to under 1%. Not deteriorating: the decline is disclosed, self-inflicted by construction the company chose, and every independent measure of customer health — database growth, dining covers, average check, out-of-town visitation — is still positive.

**The single thing the director must weigh before sizing.** Red Rock is a high-quality operating business sitting on a balance sheet that removes the margin for error. At 4.07 times net debt to operating cash profit, with roughly $10.2 billion of enterprise value against $846 million of trailing profit, a one-and-a-half-turn multiple de-rating combined with a 7% profit decline roughly halves the equity. The company is committing $375–425 million of capital in 2026 and $385 million to Durango North through summer 2027, financed partly with debt, into a revenue line growing under 1% — while the Federal Reserve's priced base case is a rate hike, not a cut, and management's own named headwind (fuel prices) is actively worsening. The quality of the franchise is not in question. The question is entirely whether the price leaves anything for the buyer.

**Economic moat: WIDE, and stable rather than widening.** The moat type is a regulatory licence combined with irreplaceable location. Nevada's gaming-district rules mean new locals casinos can effectively only be built on grandfathered, gaming-entitled parcels, and Red Rock owns 454 acres of them across six sites. The evidence that this is real and not merely asserted is in the margin: 46.2% at the property level for 2025 and rising, against a peer group at 22% to 35%. That is not a small edge; it is a structural one, and it has widened over five years, not narrowed. The most recent quarter's 113 basis-point margin decline is construction disruption at three named properties, not competitive erosion, and does not make this an eroding moat. It is marked stable rather than widening because revenue growth has stalled below 1% and returns on invested capital, at roughly 14%, are flat — good, above the cost of capital, but not compounding upward. One honest caveat: a moat that a company breaches itself is a location moat, not a franchise moat. Durango cannibalised Red Rock's own flagship badly enough to need a three-year recovery plan. The protection is against outsiders, not against the company's own next building.

**Secular threat: manageable.** There is no structural force visibly melting this earnings base. The Las Vegas valley is growing; the specific submarkets Red Rock sits in are growing faster. Online casino gaming is the theoretical threat, and Nevada is the state least likely to authorise it, since it would cannibalise the tax base the state depends on. The genuine long-run question — flagged by management's own tavern strategy — is generational: whether the next cohort of Las Vegas households treats a neighbourhood casino as their default entertainment the way the current one does. That is a real question, but it is a slow one, and nothing in these five quarters suggests it is biting yet.

**So: fear-print or value trap? Neither.** This is the third case, and it is the one the screener's corrupted inputs obscured. Red Rock is not cheap and it is not melting. It is a genuinely excellent, genuinely protected business trading at roughly twelve times enterprise value to trailing operating profit — above the highest-quality small-cap peer in its group, which carries net cash rather than $3.4 billion of net debt. The optical cheapness in the record was an artefact of three data errors. Corrected, there is no discount here to buy. There is a fine business at a full price, with the leverage to punish a disappointment.
